turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Hey, come on back. I'm gonna grab a blood pressure before Dr. Shah comes in.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh sure. I got here early because the parking garage was, uh, weirdly empty for a Tuesday, which never happens, so I just sat in the car for a minute listening to the radio.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Nice. Arm out. My sister clenches her jaw the whole drive to work and she ended up with a night guard, so I've been hearing about jaws all month.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Ha, yeah, that's sort of my department too, but I'll save the long version for the doctor, even though I usually tell it twice anyway.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 122 over 76, pulse 72, temp 36.7, oxygen 98. You're good. She'll be right in.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hi, I'm Dr. Shah. What brought you in today?

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The reason I came is jaw pain when I chew. It's not a toothache, it's up by the joint, and I went back and forth on whether the dentist should handle it, and she said to come here.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did it start? Even a rough time.

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't date it. It was last winter, or maybe the winter before, around that ice storm or after, I really don't know. What I am sure of is the pain when I chew, and it gets worse when I'm stressed.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is there a click?

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, a click, mostly on the right, right in front of the ear. Every time I open wide for a yawn or a big bite it pops, and then it settles, and I've checked it in a quiet room so I know I'm not imagining it.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Certain foods worse than others?

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Bagels, steak, anything I have to really work at. I switched to oatmeal a couple mornings just as a test, and the ache backed off, so yeah, the harder the food, the worse it is.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): What kind of work are you doing, with the stress?

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm a project manager. When a deadline hits I feel the jaw tighten by lunch, and last month's release had me at the computer till late, and those weeks were definitely louder, well, pain isn't loud, but you know.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has anyone noticed teeth grinding?

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): My husband has. He nudges me at night and says I'm grinding, this little squeak, and in the morning my teeth feel tired. He's mentioned it a bunch of times this year. I don't hear it, I'm asleep.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. I checked a few evenings with the thermometer because I was worried about infection, and it was normal every time.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Does the jaw ever lock open or closed?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No, it doesn't lock. It clicks and it aches but it always opens. I read about locking and got scared, but that part hasn't happened.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any ear pain, or a change in hearing?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No ear pain, and hearing's the same. I wondered about the ear at first because it's so close, but no.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Headaches, dizziness, anything like that?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches and no dizziness. It's the jaw and that's really the whole list.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Swelling over the joint that you've seen?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. I check in the mirror, probably too often, and it's not puffy or red.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me feel it. Open and close a few times.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tender right in front of the right ear, and I feel the click on opening. You open fully. I don't see any swelling.

[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the way I think about it, the little disc in the joint slips when the chewing muscles stay clenched, and stress keeps them tight, so you get the click and the pain. That is not an infection.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm leaning toward a panoramic x-ray today, and starting naproxen 500 milligrams twice a day for a couple of weeks.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I jump in, um. My dentist did films about a month ago and said the teeth and the bone looked fine, so I'd rather skip another x-ray. And naproxin, I took my husband's once, and my stomach was a mess for two days, so I don't want that again.

[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay, that changes my mind. Scratch the x-ray, and we are not starting naproxen. If those films were fine and the jaw isn't locking, imaging today doesn't earn it, and your stomach already voted.

[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): What I want instead is a night mouth guard while you sleep, so the grinding isn't hammering the joint. A drugstore one is fine to start, or your dentist can make a custom one.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): A guard, alright. I sleep on my side, sometimes my stomach, and I wake up a lot, so I might spit it out, but I'll try. My husband will notice if I don't put it in, he already comments on the grinding.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): And a soft diet for about three weeks. Yogurt, eggs, pasta, soup. Leave the bagels and the steak alone while this is irritated.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Soft food I can do. There's leftover soup in the fridge from Sunday, and I'll miss crusty bread more than I should admit. Is three weeks strict?
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): About three weeks, yes. You can keep taking the ibuprofen you already use when it flares. What dose is on the bottle?

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Ibuprophen, by mouth, 400 milligrams. I almost said 200, but no, I looked, the tablets are 400. I take one when the chewing pain is bad, maybe two or three times a week, not every day.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Stay with that. Don't stack it with another anti-inflammatory.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't. I don't take anything else on a regular basis, no pressure pills, not even the vitamins I keep buying and not opening.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any medication allergies?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies to medicines or foods, nothing I've ever found.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working read is temporomandibular joint irritation from the grinding, flared by chewing and stress. Provisional. We don't need a scan to call it that today.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): So not the tumor I built up at two in the morning. The click plus the internet is a bad combination, I know that's dramatic.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not a tumor, and not an infection. Come back and see me in six weeks. Sooner if it starts locking or you get a fever.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks is fine. I'll put it in my phone before I hit the parking garage, or I'll stack it on a standup and be emailing to move it.
[SEG0048] person_1 (NURSE): I can book that six-week visit at the desk. If the guard feels odd the first few nights, my sister said hers did too.

spec.situation: Person with jaw pain on chewing and clicking, worse with stress, teeth grinding noticed by partner; no fever; mouth guard and soft diet advice.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

bad.reason: Grinding at night is reported by husband, not directly by patient as certain present symptom.
bad.text: teeth grinding (category=musculoskeletal, status=present, frequency=at night, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Jaw pain was described as located up by the joint/right in front of the ear and explicitly not a toothache.
Chewing pain is worse with hard foods such as bagels and steak and improved when switching to softer food like oatmeal.
Patient reports morning teeth feel 'tired' after nighttime grinding, and husband has noticed the grinding repeatedly this year.
Negative finding missing: no redness over the jaw joint; patient said it was not puffy or red.
Doctor initially proposed panoramic x-ray today and naproxen 500 mg twice a day for a couple of weeks, but this plan was changed and canceled.
Patient reported prior dental films about a month ago showing teeth and bone looked fine, which was part of the reason to defer repeat imaging.
Patient had prior adverse reaction to naproxen: took her husband's once and had stomach upset for two days; as a result naproxen was not started.
Night guard recommendation included that an over-the-counter/drugstore guard is acceptable initially or a custom guard can be made by the dentist.
Patient reported sleep details relevant to guard tolerance: sleeps on side/sometimes stomach, wakes up a lot, and worries she might spit the guard out.
Doctor explicitly reassured that this is not an infection and not a tumor.
Patient stated she does not take any other regular medications.
Allergy documentation is partly wrong/incomplete: patient denied both medication allergies and food allergies, not just a nonspecific 'allergies' negative finding.
